title: Lassa Fever: Nigeria’s silent threat demands urgent action

analysis.time: Published on 2026-09-16. The latest infections occurred between August 16 and September 16, 2026. The report mentions epidemiological week 33, which corresponds to late August to early September 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Nigeria, specifically Ondo, Bauchi, Edo, and Benue States. The affected population includes households, patients, health workers, and communities in these areas.
analysis.event: Lassa fever is spreading in Nigeria, with 14 new confirmed cases reported during epidemiological week 33. The disease is caused by the Lassa virus, transmitted primarily through contact with infected multimammate rats, contaminated food and water, household surfaces, or airborne particles. It can also spread through contact with body fluids of infected people, particularly in healthcare settings.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) reported 1,035 cumulative infections in 2026 with 252 deaths. The case fatality rate increased to 24.4 per cent by week 33. Transmission is concentrated in several repeatedly affected states and communities. The disease can begin with mild symptoms resembling malaria, leading to delayed diagnosis and treatment.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The NCDC is actively monitoring the outbreak and has reported confirmed cases. The disease is being addressed through a One Health approach, involving communities, laboratories, and health facilities. The report highlights the need for improved diagnosis, treatment, and prevention strategies, particularly in areas with poor housing and inadequate waste management.

analysis.brief_en: Lassa fever, a viral hemorrhagic disease caused by the Lassa virus, is spreading in Nigeria, particularly in Ondo, Bauchi, Edo, and Benue States. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) reported 14 new confirmed cases during epidemiological week 33, bringing the total number of infections in 2026 to 1,035 and deaths to 252. The case fatality rate has risen to 24.4 per cent, indicating ongoing challenges in diagnosis and treatment. Transmission occurs primarily through contact with infected multimammate rats, contaminated food and water, household surfaces, or airborne particles, and can also spread through body fluids of infected individuals in healthcare settings. Early symptoms often mimic malaria, leading to delayed medical attention. Experts emphasize the need for heightened clinical suspicion and community-based prevention efforts, as poor housing and inadequate waste management increase exposure risks. The disease is being addressed through a One Health approach, recognizing the interconnectedness of human health, animal populations, and environmental conditions.
